**Observation Log:**

- [FACT] The user has been teaching for over 10 years.
- [PREFERENCE] The user feels it is unfair that teaching experience alone cannot lead to promotion to associate professor.
- [PREFERENCE] The user believes they are more capable than many associate professors at their university.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Teaching experience typically cannot substitute for required qualifications to become an associate professor in a university.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Each university has specific requirements for promotion, usually including advanced degrees, research and publication accomplishments, and other essential experience related to the field of study.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Strong teaching experience is highly valued but usually not sufficient on its own for promotion to associate professor.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Academic promotion is based on a combination of criteria including research, teaching, and service to the university or community.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Candidates must meet minimum academic qualifications specified by the university, such as holding a specific advanced degree or certificate in the relevant field.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The user may want to inquire about the specific promotion criteria at their university to determine eligibility and work on developing necessary qualifications for promotion.
- [PREFERENCE] The user expresses frustration that universities prioritize degrees and research over actual teaching ability.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Research is a significant component of the job expectations for associate professorships as it demonstrates an understanding of the field and an ability to contribute to it.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Promotion committees assess candidates' overall job performance, including research, teaching, mentoring, and other factors, rather than relying on a single criterion.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Universities are increasingly recognizing the importance of quality teaching by creating teaching-focused promotions and awards.
